name: Evidence Extraction Tables
title: Evidence Extraction Tables
answer: Evidence extraction tables are structured summaries that pull key claims, study designs, populations, interventions, outcomes, and effect sizes from primary research into a comparable grid. They sit inside literature review and evidence synthesis workflows, turning scattered papers into a single view for screening, appraisal, and synthesis. On this site, the practice draws on a library of 135 research papers and 10,555 extracted claims, so a table is not a loose note but a traceable index of what each source actually says. The scope covers both human-led extraction and machine-assisted extraction, but the table itself remains the shared artifact for reviewers.

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables are structured summaries that pull key claims, study designs, populations, interventions, outcomes, and effect sizes from primary research into a comparable grid. They sit inside literature review and evidence synthesis workflows, turning scattered papers into a single view for screening, appraisal, and synthesis. On this site, the practice draws on a library of 135 research papers and 10,555 extracted claims, so a table is not a loose note but a traceable index of what each source actually says. The scope covers both human-led extraction and machine-assisted extraction, but the table itself remains the shared artifact for reviewers.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of reference managers, spreadsheet tools, and dedicated extraction platforms, with the site's catalogue of 732 AI tools and 801 scientific models available as a map of what can be used. A typical setup stores PDFs and bibliographic data in one place, then links each table row to the original paper rather than to a secondary search tool. Because content on this site never links to the Consensus search tool, the infrastructure is built around direct access to source documents, DOIs, and local or institutional repositories. Lightweight databases or structured files hold the extracted fields so they can be filtered, sorted, and exported.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Extraction begins by defining the question and a codebook of fields, such as sample size, comparator, outcome measure, and risk of bias. Reviewers then read each paper and enter values into the table, often with a second person checking a sample for agreement. Machine assistance can pre-fill fields or flag sentences that contain claims, but a human still verifies the entry against the full text. The site's 10,555 extracted claims show the result of this method at scale, where each row is a claim tied to a specific paper and location.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on provenance, version control, and error. Every cell should carry a source link or page reference so a reader can return to the original paper, and the site's practice of linking to the original paper rather than a search tool supports that audit trail. Extraction tables can introduce bias if fields are inconsistently coded or if negative results are dropped, so the table needs a clear protocol and a record of who entered what and when. Copyright and licensing matter when sharing extracted text, and reviewers should paraphrase or quote only within fair use or the paper's terms.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward semi-automated extraction that still keeps a human in the loop, with models proposing rows and reviewers confirming or correcting them. Tables are likely to become more connected to living evidence systems, where new papers update the same grid instead of starting a fresh review. As the site's library grows beyond 135 papers and 10,555 claims, the challenge will be keeping tables consistent across time and across different review teams. The likely endpoint is a reusable, versioned evidence base that can feed multiple syntheses without losing the link back to each source.
